title: Your site was built for Google, but now AI is the one reading it
excerpt: ChatGPT and Gemini now answer in place of the click. See what AIs need to find on your site to cite your business, and what is stopping them today.
content:
Try a quick test before you keep reading. Open ChatGPT and ask which is the best company in your industry in your city. Then ask again, swapping "best" for "most trustworthy". If your company's name didn't come up in either answer, that's not bad luck. It's that your site wasn't written for whoever is doing the answering.

For many years the rule was simple: get on Google's first page and hope for the click. That rule isn't dead, but it's no longer the only one. Today a huge share of searches end with no click at all, because the answer shows up ready on the screen, summarized by an artificial intelligence that read dozens of sites and picked a few to cite. The question that matters has moved. It's no longer just "is my site ranking well". It's "is my site being cited".

What GEO is and why it doesn't replace SEO

GEO stands for Generative Engine Optimization. It's the set of content, structure and code decisions that make an artificial intelligence understand your site, trust it and use your name when it answers someone. SEO is still the foundation, because AIs feed on what search engines index. GEO is the new layer, the one that decides whether, after finding your site, the machine will consider your business worth mentioning.

In one line: SEO competes for position, GEO competes for citation. If you only take care of the first one, you're playing half the game.

Five signs your site has fallen behind

  1. Your key information is inside images. Price, what sets you apart, address and opening hours all became pretty graphics. An AI doesn't read graphics, it reads text.
  2. The site answers everything with "get in touch". If the only concrete answer on your page is a WhatsApp button, there's nothing there to cite.
  3. No new content has gone up in over a year. Generative systems favor living sources. A site that stands still looks like a business that stands still.
  4. The page is slow to load on mobile. Slowness drops your Google ranking and makes crawlers give up before they finish reading.
  5. Nobody signs the content. No author, no CNPJ (Brazilian company registration number), no address, no proof: the site becomes just another anonymous text on the internet. Anonymous doesn't get cited.

Why older sites get stuck right at this point

Many of the sites live today were born in visual builders that prioritize the on-screen effect. The result is a beautiful, heavy page built almost entirely with JavaScript, where the text only exists after the browser finishes running the code. Visitors don't even notice. An AI's crawler, which most of the time doesn't run JavaScript, shows up, finds a practically empty page and leaves.

Add to that the lack of structured data, the snippet of code that tells the machine "this is a business, this is an article, this is the author, this is the address", and you have the complete recipe for invisibility. The site exists for people and doesn't exist for machines.

What changes when the site is built for both

  • The content arrives ready on the first load, without depending on code to show up.
  • Each page answers a real question, with the answer in the very first sentence and the details below.
  • Structured data tells the machine who the business is, what it does, where it is and who wrote the content.
  • The blog keeps feeding the site with new material, which is what keeps the brand showing up in answers.
  • Speed and mobile readability stop being a technical detail and become a business advantage.

What staying invisible costs you

This math is uncomfortable, but it's worth doing. Think about how many people a month search for what you sell. Assume that only a tenth of those searches now end inside an AI, with no click at all. Now multiply that by your average ticket and your close rate. Whatever number you get is what your business leaves on the table every month, quietly. There's no report for sales lost because you weren't cited.

When updating your site is not the priority

To be honest: not every business needs to touch its site right now. If you sell by referral and your calendar is full, if your revenue comes from closed contracts, or if your site is just a business card for people who have already decided to buy, the investment can wait. An update makes sense when the site needs to bring in new people, not when it just confirms the ones who already arrived. If the bottleneck today is inside the operation and not in bringing in leads, the right investment may be something else: a custom system to replace the spreadsheet only one person understands.

How an update like this works

  1. Diagnosis. We check what Google indexes today and what an AI actually sees when it visits your domain.
  2. Content architecture. We map the questions your customers ask and turn each one into a page or section.
  3. Technical rebuild. The site is rebuilt with fast delivery, machine-readable HTML and structured data.
  4. A blog with its own dashboard. You publish on your own, without depending on anyone and with no platform monthly fee.
  5. Measurement. We track ranking, traffic and, above all, mentions of the brand in generated answers.

A website is not a brochure. It's the source that decides whether your business will be remembered when someone asks a machine who to trust.

Where to start

Start with the test from the first paragraph. Ask two different AIs about your industry and write down who got cited. If competitors show up and you don't, you already have the answer you needed, and it cost nothing.
